templates.subject: Physics
templates.template: A bus starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at {a} m s⁻² along a straight road. Find its velocity after {t} s and the distance it covers in that time.

solutionChain.statement: u = 0 m s⁻¹ (starts from rest), a = {a} m s⁻², t = {t} s
solutionChain.justification: Write every given with its unit before touching a formula. Half the lost marks in this unit start here.
First equation of motion links v, u, a and t — no distance term needed.
Second equation of motion gives distance over the same interval.

misconceptions.statement: Used s = at² and dropped the ½.
misconceptions.feedback: You used s = at². The ½ in s = ut + ½at² comes from averaging velocity across the interval — without it the distance doubles.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: at is a velocity and multiplying a velocity by time gives a distance, so the shape looks right.

misconceptions.statement: Gave the velocity where the distance was asked for.
misconceptions.feedback: That is v, not s. Read what the question asks for last — the marks are for the distance.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: v = at is the first thing you compute, so it is sitting at the top of your page when you stop.

templates.subject: Physics
templates.template: A block of mass {m} kg is pulled along a horizontal floor by a horizontal force of {F} N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between block and floor is {mu}. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Find the acceleration of the block.

solutionChain.statement: m = {m} kg, F = {F} N, μ = {mu}, g = 9.8 m s⁻²
solutionChain.justification: μ is a ratio — it has no unit. Say so explicitly; examiners look for it.
On a horizontal floor with a horizontal pull, the normal reaction carries the whole weight.
Kinetic friction is proportional to the normal reaction, not to the applied force.
Friction opposes the motion, so it subtracts along the direction of travel.
Newton's second law, applied to the net force — never to the applied force alone.

misconceptions.statement: Ignored friction and used the applied force as the net force.
misconceptions.feedback: You divided the applied force by the mass. Newton's second law takes the NET force — friction of {mu*m*9.8} N is still acting the whole time.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: F = ma is stated with an F, and the applied force is the F the question gives you a number for.

misconceptions.statement: Took friction as μ × applied force.
misconceptions.feedback: Friction is μN, not μF. The normal reaction is what presses the surfaces together — the pull is horizontal and does not change it here.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both are forces measured in newtons, so multiplying by μ feels like the same operation either way.

templates.subject: Physics
templates.template: A car of mass {m} kg moving at {u} m s⁻¹ is brought to rest by its brakes in a distance of {s} m. Find the average braking force.

solutionChain.statement: m = {m} kg, u = {u} m s⁻¹, v = 0 m s⁻¹, s = {s} m
solutionChain.justification: Brought to rest means the final velocity is zero — write it down as a given, do not carry it in your head.
The energy the brakes have to remove is the kinetic energy the car starts with.

solutionChain.statement: Work done by brakes = ΔKE = 0 − ½mu²; magnitude = ½mu²
solutionChain.justification: Work–energy theorem: net work equals the change in kinetic energy.
Work is force × distance along the line of the force, so the average force is the work divided by the stopping distance.

misconceptions.statement: Dropped the ½ from the kinetic energy.
misconceptions.feedback: Kinetic energy is ½mv², not mv². Your force comes out exactly twice too large — a factor of 2 is a whole mark.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Momentum is mv with no fraction in front, so ½ looks like decoration.

misconceptions.feedback: You used mu/s. That mixes momentum with a distance — check the units: kg m s⁻¹ ÷ m is not a newton. A unit check catches this in five seconds.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both mu and ½mu² describe 'how much motion there is', so either can feel like the right starting quantity.

templates.subject: Physics
templates.template: A trolley of mass {m1} kg moving at {u1} m s⁻¹ collides head-on with a stationary trolley of mass {m2} kg. The two lock together after the collision. Find their common velocity.

solutionChain.statement: m₁ = {m1} kg, u₁ = {u1} m s⁻¹, m₂ = {m2} kg, u₂ = 0 m s⁻¹
solutionChain.justification: Stationary means u₂ = 0 m s⁻¹ — an explicit given, not an assumption.
No external horizontal force acts during the collision, so momentum is conserved.
They lock together, so afterwards there is one object of combined mass.
Momentum after equals momentum before; divide by the combined mass to get the common velocity.

misconceptions.statement: Divided by the second mass instead of the total mass.
misconceptions.feedback: After the collision the moving object is both trolleys together, so the mass to divide by is m₁ + m₂ = {m1+m2} kg.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: It looks like the momentum is being 'handed over' to the second trolley.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving only works when the two masses are equal. Here they are {m1} kg and {m2} kg, so the share is set by the mass ratio.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Two objects, so 'split it in two' is the fast intuition.

templates.subject: Physics
templates.template: A planet has mass {M} × 10²⁴ kg and radius {R} × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², find the escape velocity from its surface.

solutionChain.statement: M = {M} × 10²⁴ kg, R = {R} × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²
solutionChain.justification: Convert the powers of ten into the working before you press a single calculator key.
Surface gravity from the planet's own mass and radius.
Escape velocity is the speed at which kinetic energy exactly cancels the gravitational potential energy.

misconceptions.statement: Used orbital velocity instead of escape velocity.
misconceptions.feedback: √(GM/R) is the ORBITAL velocity. Escape velocity carries the extra factor of 2 inside the root: v_e = √2 × v_orbital.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The two formulas differ by one character, and both describe 'the speed you need'.

misconceptions.feedback: The 10²⁴ and 10⁶ are part of the numbers, not decoration. Substitute them before you divide — a dimension check on the answer would have flagged this.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Powers of ten look like formatting rather than quantity.

templates.subject: Physics
templates.problemTypeLabel: Calorimetry with a change of state
templates.template: How much heat is needed to convert {m} g of ice at 0 °C completely into water at {T} °C? Take the specific latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

solutionChain.statement: m = {m} g = {m}/1000 kg, L_f = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔT = {T} K
solutionChain.justification: Convert grams to kilograms first — every constant here is per kilogram. A temperature DIFFERENCE in °C equals the same number in K.
Melting happens at constant temperature: all the heat goes into the change of state.

solutionChain.statement: Q₂ = mcΔT (warming the melted water from 0 °C to {T} °C)
solutionChain.justification: Only after the ice has fully melted does the temperature start to rise.
The two stages happen one after the other, so the heats add.

misconceptions.feedback: Both constants are per KILOGRAM, so {m} g must become {m}/1000 kg. Your answer is 1000 times too big — that is the single most common slip in this unit.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The question gives grams, so grams feel like the natural unit to work in.

misconceptions.feedback: You only warmed the water. Melting the ice at 0 °C takes energy first — that is the mL_f term, and it is worth its own mark.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Nothing visible changes temperature during melting, so it looks like nothing is happening.

templates.subject: Physics
templates.template: An object is placed {u} cm in front of a converging lens of focal length {f} cm. Find the image distance and the magnification.

solutionChain.statement: Object distance u = −{u} cm, focal length f = +{f} cm (real-is-positive convention: distances measured against the incoming light are negative)
solutionChain.justification: State the sign convention in writing. Sign-convention marks (PH-U03) are lost silently otherwise.
Thin-lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, rearranged for v.
Magnification is the ratio of image to object distance; a value below 1 means the image is smaller.

misconceptions.statement: Added the reciprocals instead of subtracting.
misconceptions.feedback: With u = −{u} cm the formula gives 1/v = 1/f + 1/u where 1/u is negative. Adding a positive 1/u puts the image on the wrong side of the lens.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f uses a plus, and the two get stored in memory as one formula.

misconceptions.statement: Gave the focal length as the image distance.
misconceptions.feedback: v equals f only when the object is at infinity. Here the object is {u} cm away, so v is larger than f.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The ray diagram everyone draws first is the parallel-rays-to-focus one.

templates.subject: Physics
templates.template: A wire of length {L} m and cross-sectional area {A} × 10⁻⁷ m² is made of a metal of resistivity {rho} × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. It is connected across a {V} V supply. Find the resistance of the wire and the current through it.

solutionChain.statement: L = {L} m, A = {A} × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = {rho} × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, V = {V} V
solutionChain.justification: Write the powers of ten into the substitution, not into your head.
Resistance grows with length and falls with cross-section — the defining relation for resistivity.
Ohm's law, applied once the resistance is known.

misconceptions.statement: Multiplied by area instead of dividing.
misconceptions.feedback: R = ρL/A. A thicker wire carries current more easily, so area belongs on the bottom. Check it against the physical story before you substitute.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Every other quantity in the formula multiplies, so the division looks like the odd one out.

misconceptions.statement: Multiplied V by R instead of dividing.
misconceptions.feedback: I = V/R. Multiplying gives you V × R, whose unit is V Ω — not an ampere. One unit check kills this.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: V = IR is the version most people memorise, and rearranging under time pressure flips the operation.
